Article content: {"plain_text":"There is a deeply offensive yet pervasive trend that you’ve probably been a victim of: receiving AI-generated writing disguised as human creation.
Students are submitting ChatGPT essays, users are botting replies on social networks, and mass cold outreach is saturated by a wave of AI thoughtlessness. And perpetrators of this behavior shamelessly shrug under the masquerade of efficiency. But like most folks on the consuming end, as soon as I sense something is slop, I become utterly uninterested in what it tries to convey. Whatever useful substance it contains is ignored. I’ve recently resorted to “send the prompt, not the slop” as the strategy when I encounter AI writing.
Here’s why we instinctively reject slop and thus cannot rely on LLMs for important, original communication. A fundamental property of models is that they tend to expand on the prompt, naturally making sentences verbose, obtuse, and soulless. At the risk of not giving enough, models always give more than you actually need and can digest, ballooning your original prompt to a bloated artifact.
A shorter output equals a lower probability of continuing the conversation, therefore less propensity for further token consumption, contradicting the bottom line of the model makers. Can you remember the last time you saw a succinct response? However, a lengthy response is directly at odds with what you’re asking of the recipient.
When you ask another person to read something, what you’re really asking for is their time, attention, and unique processing in the form of a human perspective. You’re asking for them to be in communion with your thoughts as a single-threaded being. So sending anyone slop–or the worst form, a simulacrum of your voice transmitted–is doing their intelligence a disservice. You’re requesting an unbalanced exchange and saying: “I do not wish to take the effort to condense or clarify my thoughts, but you should nevertheless take the full effort to engage.” The intentionality is undignified, and the lack of care dissolves all trust.
While AI is an effective tool to help you intake and synthesize swaths of information, the majority of current usage outputs vapid representations of what you truly mean. This is because original, creative thinking and writing will always be out-of-distribution and non-obvious. Outsourcing your writing to AI promotes the decay of your intelligence, regressing it to the mean.
So even with AI accessible, I believe in the intrinsic value in getting words on the page and dire consequences if the muscle is allowed to atrophy. George Orwell said: "If people cannot write well, they cannot think well, and if they cannot think well, others will do their thinking for them." In this case, once the models do most of the thinking, we will simply act as the messengers who ping pong their outputs.
We often conflate the fact that something can be done better by something else with the fact that the thing is no longer worth our time. But even with the invention of calculators, we still educate kids on how to do math, because the point of intellectual activity is rarely learning the activity itself. Instead, it’s the cognitive rigor that is ingrained implicitly. Another lens is what makes something valuable. In art, the process and craft are what assign significance to human production, perhaps weighing more than what the image actually looks like. Otherwise, Midjourney generations would be sold for millions.
It’s been said that the medium is the message; now we will say that the process is the message. More than ever, it is our intentionality, care, and craft that will be considered by the recipient as centrally as the content itself. At a time when mediocre writing is exploding and good writing is dwindling, organic non-LLM-coded content will be the proxy of independent, creative thinking. It will be the dominant mechanism for forming trust.
